claim: The superior colliculus receives approximately 85% of retinal outputs in rodents.
source: One of the major retinorecipient areas is the superior colliculus, which receives approximately 85% of the retinal outputs in rodents (Ellis et al., 2016; Hofbauer and Dräger, 1985; Linden and Perry, 1983; Vaney et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ellis et al., 2016; Hofbauer and Dräger, 1985; Linden and Perry, 1983; Vaney et al., 1981).

claim: Each neuron of the superficial superior colliculus has been estimated to receive input from on average six retinal ganglion cells.
source: Each neuron of the superficial superior colliculus has been estimated to receive input from on average six retinal ganglion cells (Chandrasekaran et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chandrasekaran et al., 2007.

claim: The mammalian retina output consists of over 30 different ganglion cell types.
source: The output of the mammalian retina, the first stage of visual processing, consists of over 30 different ganglion cell types which can be distinguished by their dendritic anatomy, response properties, or molecular markers (Baden et al., 2016; Bae et al., 2018; Dhande et al., 2015; Farrow and Masland, 2011; Levick, 1967; Martersteck et al., 2017; Roska and Werblin, 2001; Sanes and Masland, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Cells innervating the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit had larger dendritic trees (median: 279 μm) than cells innervating the colliculo-pulvinar circuit (median: 190 μm).
source: First, cells innervating the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit had larger dendritic trees (median: 279 μm) than the cells innervating the colliculo-pulvinar circuit (median: 190 μm; p<0.01, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Wilcoxon rank sum test; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the data and statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.01), as shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The colliculo-pulvinar circuit showed strong bias for sampling from neurons stratifying between (55.6%) and above (29.3%) the ChAT-bands.
source: While the colliculo-pulvinar circuit showed strong bias for sampling from neurons stratifying between (55.6%) and above (29.3%) the ChAT-bands, the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit sampled more evenly from each stratification level (bistratified 14.5%, below ChAT-bands 25.3%, between 39.0%, above 21.2%; Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing percentages of cells at different stratification levels, as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The colliculo-parabigeminal circuit sampled more evenly from each stratification level (bistratified 14.5%, below ChAT-bands 25.3%, between 39.0%, above 21.2%).
source: While the colliculo-pulvinar circuit showed strong bias for sampling from neurons stratifying between (55.6%) and above (29.3%) the ChAT-bands, the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit sampled more evenly from each stratification level (bistratified 14.5%, below ChAT-bands 25.3%, between 39.0%, above 21.2%; Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing percentages of cells at different stratification levels, as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 14 of the 37 classes of retinal ganglion cells contained at least 1% of the ganglion cells from the data set.
source: This analysis revealed that 14 of the 37 classes of retinal ganglion cells contained at least 1% of the ganglion cells from our data set, suggesting that a limited set of retinal ganglion cell types are sampled by the colliculo-pulvinar and colliculo-parabigeminal circuits (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the data set, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Clusters 3, 4, 7 and 13 preferentially innervated the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit.
source: We found that clusters 3, 4, 7 and 13 preferentially innervated the colliculo-parabigeminal (cluster 3 p=0.0322 | 0.0221; cluster 4 p=0.0009 | 10−5; cluster 7 p=0.0483 | 0.0358; cluster 13 p=0.0009 | 10−9, bootstrap analysis | two-proportion z-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (bootstrap analysis and two-proportion z-test) showing significant p-values.

claim: Clusters 2, 5, 10 and 11 preferentially innervate the colliculo-pulvinar circuit.
source: and clusters 2, 5, 10 and 11 preferentially innervate the colliculo-pulvinar circuit (cluster 2 p=0.0009 | 0.0001; cluster 5 p=0.0217 | 0.0001; cluster 10 p=0.0483 | 0.0001; cluster 11 p=0.0241 | 0.0299, bootstrap analysis | two-proportion z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (bootstrap analysis and two-proportion z-test) showing significant p-values.

claim: Six cell types (cluster 1, 6, 8, 9, 12 and 14) innervate both circuits more evenly.
source: The remaining six cell types (cluster 1, 6, 8, 9, 12 and 14) were found to innervate both circuits more evenly (cluster 1 p=0.9933 | 0.9794; cluster 6 p=0.3717 | 0.0513; cluster 8 p=0.5350 | 0.2452; cluster 9 p=0.6640 | 0.4568; cluster 12 p=0.9933 | 0.9731; cluster 14 p=0.8462 | 0.7091, bootstrap analysis | two-proportion z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant p-values, indicating no bias.

claim: Cluster 4 consists of CART+, ON-OFF direction-selective cells.
source: Cluster 4 (EM C-37) consists of the CART+, ON-OFF direction-selective cells.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular identification (CART+) and anatomical classification.

claim: Around half of all rabies-labeled cells innervating the two circuits are alpha-cells (colliculo-parabigeminal median: 42%, n = 3 retinas; colliculo-pulvinar median: 53%, n = 4 retinas).
source: We found that around half of all rabies-labeled cells innervating the two circuits are alpha-cells (colliculo-parabigeminal median: 42%, n = 3 retinas; colliculo-pulvinar median: 53%, n = 4 retinas; Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from molecular analysis, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transient ON-cells mostly innervate the colliculo-pulvinar circuit (parabigeminal vs pulvinar median: 4% vs 17%; p<0.05 two proportion z-test).
source: In contrast, transient ON-cells mostly innervate the colliculo-pulvinar circuit (parabigeminal vs pulvinar median: 4% vs 17%; p<0.05 two proportion z-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical testing (two proportion z-test, p<0.05).

claim: Sustained ON-cells are almost exclusively labeled in the parabigeminal circuits (parabigeminal vs pulvinar median: 10% vs <0.5%; p<0.05 two proportion z-test).
source: while sustained ON-cells are almost exclusively labeled in the parabigeminal circuits (parabigeminal vs pulvinar median: 10% vs <0.5%; p<0.05 two proportion z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical testing (two proportion z-test, p<0.05).

claim: Double-labeled neurons (GCaMP6s+ and CART+) are found almost exclusively after retrograde tracing from the parabigeminal nucleus (median: 6.9% of all GCaMP6s-postive cells, range: 4.3% to 9.1%, n = 3 retinas).
source: Double-labeled neurons (GCaMP6s+ and CART+) are found almost exclusively after retrograde tracing from the parabigeminal nucleus (Figure 3E; median: 6.9% of all GCaMP6s-postive cells, range: 4.3% to 9.1%, n = 3 retinas).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from molecular analysis, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the pulvinar experiments, a negligible percentage of the labeled ganglion cells are CART+ (median: 1.3%, range: 0% to 2.1%, n = 6 retinas).
source: In the pulvinar experiments, a negligible percentage of the labeled ganglion cells are CART+ (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; median: 1.3%, range: 0% to 2.1%, n = 6 retinas).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from molecular analysis, as shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The visual responses to the 'chirp' stimulus were consistent with the predicted response based on published data.
source: We found that the visual responses to the 'chirp' stimulus were consistent with the predicted response based on published data (Baden et al., 2016) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published data (Baden et al., 2016) and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Sustained ON and OFF-alpha cells show a strong asymmetric decrease of dendritic size along the naso-temporal axis.
source: It has previously been demonstrated that sustained ON and OFF-alpha cells, but not transient OFF-alpha cells show a strong asymmetric decrease of dendritic size along the naso-temporal axis (Bleckert et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bleckert et al., 2014).

claim: The two sustained types show a negative correlation along the naso-temporal axis with small neurons found preferentially in the temporal retina.
source: We found that the two sustained types show the previously reported negative correlation along the naso-temporal axis with small neurons found preferentially in the temporal retina (Figure 5F–G)
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5F-G, confirming previously reported findings.

claim: Transient OFF-alpha cells do not show any asymmetry in dendritic size along the naso–temporal axis.
source: As expected, we did not observe any asymmetry in dendritic size of transient OFF-alpha cells along the naso–temporal axis (Figure 5H–L) (Bleckert et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5H-L and citation to Bleckert et al., 2014.

claim: Transient OFF-alpha cells display an increasing response duration along the ventral – dorsal axis of the retina.
source: In addition, while transient OFF-alpha cells do not show an asymmetric distribution of dendritic size, they do display an increasing response duration along the ventral – dorsal axis of the retina (Warwick et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Warwick et al., 2018.

claim: A similar increase in response duration for transient OFF-alpha neurons along the ventral-dorsal axis was found, consistent with Warwick et al. (2018).
source: We found a similar increase in response duration for transient OFF-alpha neurons along this axis of the retina that was consistent, though with a weaker correlation, with Warwick et al. (2018) (Figure 5M–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5M-P and comparison with published data (Warwick et al., 2018).

claim: Neurons in both the pulvinar and parabigeminal nucleus responded reliably to a set of visual stimuli including a large fast moving square, a small fast moving spot, and expanding discs.
source: We found that neurons in both the posterior pulvinar and parabigeminal nucleus responded reliably to a set of visual stimuli (Figure 6G) that includes: a large fast moving square ('big-fast', 53° side length, 150°/s); a small, fast moving spot ('small-fast', 4° diameter, 150°/s) and expanding discs (expanding from 2° to 50° of diameter within 300 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings, as shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The percentages of responding units differed for different stimuli between the parabigeminal nucleus and the pulvinar.
source: However, the percentages of responding units (maximal response > mean spontaneous firing rate + two std) differed for the different stimuli between the parabigeminal nucleus and the pulvinar (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of response data, as shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A large fraction of parabigeminal neurons showed a preference for one or two directions of motion.
source: A large fraction of parabigeminal neurons showed a preference for one or two directions of motion (Figure 6I and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings, as shown in Figure 6I and K.

claim: Direction-selectivity was not present in pulvinar neurons.
source: This direction-selectivity was not present in pulvinar neurons (Figure 6J and K; p<0.05 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparing the DSI distributions for the two nuclei).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<0.05), as shown in Figure 6J and K.

claim: Neurons in both the pulvinar and parabigeminal nucleus responded during the expansion phase of a black expanding disc stimulus.
source: Neurons in both the pulvinar and parabigeminal nucleus responded during the expansion phase of this stimulus, and there was no difference in the distribution of response strengths between the two populations of neurons (p>0.05 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; Figure 6L–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p>0.05), as shown in Figure 6L-M.

claim: Only the ON-OFF direction-selective cells in cluster 4 were direction-selective.
source: As expected, only the ON-OFF direction-selective cells in cluster 4 were direction-selective and none of the cell types showed evidence of orientation-selectivity (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from retinal recordings, as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The transient OFF-alpha cells (cluster 6) and cells in cluster 5 displayed the strongest responses during the period of expansion of a black expanding disc.
source: The transient OFF-alpha cells (cluster 6), and cells in cluster 5 displayed the strongest responses during the period of expansion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from retinal recordings analyzing responses to expanding disc stimuli.

claim: Both circuits receive input from cell types that respond during the expansion phase of the expanding disc stimulus.
source: First, both circuits receive input from cell types that respond during the expansion phase of the expanding disc stimulus (Figure 2 and Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on integration of data from circuit tracing (Figure 2) and physiological recordings (Figure 7).

claim: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells have a strong preference for the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit.
source: Second, in accordance with different direction-selectivity of the two target nuclei (Figure 6), we found that direction-selective retinal ganglion cells have a strong preference for the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on integration of data from circuit tracing (Figure 2) and physiological recordings in target nuclei (Figure 6).

claim: The 'chirp' stimulus produces robust responses in most retinal ganglion cells but fails to illicit responses in either the posterior pulvinar or the parabigeminal nucleus.
source: The 'chirp' stimulus produces robust responses in most retinal ganglion cells but fails to illicit responses in either the posterior pulvinar, or the parabigeminal nucleus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses in retina and target nuclei, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The colliculo-parabigeminal and colliculo-pulvinar circuit together sample from a limited set (14 of 37) of retinal ganglion cell types.
source: First, the colliculo-parabigeminal and colliculo-pulvinar circuit together sample from a limited set (14 of 37) of retinal ganglion cell types (Bae et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of the data set and comparison with published cell type classifications (Bae et al., 2018).

claim: Four putative ganglion cell types show a strong preference for the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit, and four others for the colliculo-pulvinar circuit, while six other types are more equally sampled by both circuits.
source: Second, there is a clear preference in the set of retinal ganglion cell types providing input to each circuit. While four putative ganglion cell types show a strong preference for the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit, and four others for the colliculo-pulvinar circuit, six other types are more equally sampled by both circuits.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis and statistical testing of circuit-specific sampling biases.

claim: Some response properties of neurons in downstream targets can be explained by the different and shared sampling biases of each retinal ganglion cell type by each collicular output pathway.
source: Third, some response properties of neurons in downstream targets can be explained by the different and shared sampling biases of each retinal ganglion cell type by each collicular output pathway, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on integration and comparison of data from circuit tracing and physiological recordings in retina and target nuclei.

claim: HSV has a strictly synaptic uptake mechanism that prevents infection of passing axons.
source: First, HSV has a strictly synaptic uptake mechanism that prevents infection of passing axons, ensuring that we labeled neurons that synapse within the pulvinar or parabigeminal nucleus (Antinone and Smith, 2010; McGavern and Kang, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Antinone and Smith, 2010; McGavern and Kang, 2011).

claim: G-deleted rabies has been demonstrated to reliably label retinal ganglion cells innervating the superior colliculus, dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus or medial terminal nucleus.
source: Second, G-deleted rabies has been demonstrated to reliably label retinal ganglion cells innervating the superior colliculus, dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus or medial terminal nucleus (Cruz-Martín et al., 2014; Ellis et al., 2016; Farrow et al., 2013; Rompani et al., 2017; Yonehara et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature demonstrating the reliability of the method.

claim: Injection of EnvA-coated rabies virus into the superior colliculus without previous injection of HSV resulted in no labeling of retinal ganglion cells in the retina or neurons in the superior colliculus.
source: Finally, injection of EnvA-coated rabies virus into the superior colliculus, without previous injection of HSV-rabiesG-TVA-mCherry into either the pulvinar or parabigeminal nucleus resulted in no labeling of retinal ganglion cells in the retina or neurons in the superior colliculus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental control data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Ntsr1-GN209Cre mouse line ensured labeling of wide-field neurons of the superior colliculus that project to the lateral pulvinar and not adjacent thalamic nuclei.
source: To infect neurons projecting to the lateral pulvinar we utilized a floxed version of the HSV virus (hEF1a-LS1L-TVA950-T2A-RabiesG-IRES-mCherry) in combination with the Ntsr1-GN209Cre mouse line, which ensured labeling of wide-field neurons of the superior colliculus that project to the lateral pulvinar and not adjacent thalamic nuclei (Gale and Murphy, 2018; Gale and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gale and Murphy, 2018; Gale and Murphy, 2014) describing the specificity of this mouse line.

claim: The dendritic field diameters of labeled cells ranged from 57 to 468 µm (median: 194 µm), similar to the reported range of 80 to 530 µm.
source: Our data set contains cells with dendritic field diameters ranging from 57 to 468 µm (median: 194 µm), similar to the reported range of 80 to 530 µm (Badea and Nathans, 2004; Bae et al., 2018; Coombs et al., 2006; Kong et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the data and comparison with published literature.

claim: The differences in size between the colliculo-parabigeminal and colliculo-pulvinar circuit are not due to a bias in the retinotopic location of the sampled ganglion cells.
source: We found that these differences are not due to a bias in the retinotopic location of the sampled cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of spatial distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

source: Both circuits sample from sustained and transient OFF-alpha cells (parabigeminal vs pulvinar median: 13% vs 20% sustained; 32% vs 29% transient OFF-cells; 100% corresponds to all GFP+ cells).

claim: Direction-selective responses in the superior colliculus rely on the inhibitory output of starburst amacrine cells.
source: First, it has been demonstrated that direction-selective responses in the superior colliculus rely on the inhibitory output of starburst amacrine cells (Shi et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Shi et al., 2017).

claim: Starburst amacrine cells are responsible for the direction-selective responses of ON-OFF and ON direction-selective ganglion cells.
source: where starburst amacrine cells are responsible for the direction-selective responses of ON-OFF and ON direction-selective ganglion cells (Euler et al., 2002; Fried et al., 2002; Hillier et al., 2017; Pei et al., 2015; Yonehara et al., 2016; Yonehara et al., 2013; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Starburst amacrine cells have not been implicated in mediating the direction-selective responses of highly asymmetric retinal ganglion cell types including the Fmini and JAM-B neurons.
source: However, starburst amacrine cells have not been implicated in mediating the direction-selective responses of highly asymmetric retinal ganglion cell types including the Fmini and JAM-B neurons (Joesch and Meister, 2016; Kim et al., 2008; Rousso et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Joesch and Meister, 2016; Kim et al., 2008; Rousso et al., 2016).

claim: The direction-selectivity of Fmini neurons is highly speed dependent, with a peak selectivity at 585 µm/s and negligible selectivity at speeds greater than 1300 µm/s.
source: Second, unlike ON-OFF direction-selective neurons, the direction-selectivity of Fmini neurons is highly speed dependent, with a peak selectivity at 585 µm/s and negligible selectivity at speeds greater than 1300 µm/s (Rousso et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Rousso et al., 2016).

claim: Direction-selective responses in the parabigeminal nucleus were recorded at speeds equivalent to more than 1500 µm/s on the retina.
source: Direction-selective responses in the parabigeminal nucleus were recorded at speeds equivalent to more than 1500 µm/s on the retina.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: The direction-selectivity of JAM-B neurons is highly dependent on each neuron's individual dendritic asymmetry.
source: Kim et al. (2008) reported that the direction-selectivity of JAM-B neurons is highly dependent on each neuron's individual dendritic asymmetry
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Kim et al., 2008).

claim: The direction-selective, but not orientation-selective, responses of JAM-B cells are sensitive to light conditions.
source: while it has been reported that the direction-selective, but not orientation-selective, responses of JAM-B cells are sensitive to light conditions (Joesch and Meister, 2016; Nath and Schwartz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Joesch and Meister, 2016; Nath and Schwartz, 2017).

claim: The two neural circuits investigated each mediate visually guided aversive behaviors.
source: The two neural circuits investigated here are each known to mediate visually guided aversive behaviors (Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015).

claim: Neurons in the pulvinar respond poorly to large stimuli but responded to small, slowly moving stimuli.
source: We found that neurons in the pulvinar respond poorly to large stimuli, but responded to small, slowly moving stimuli
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: Small, slowly moving stimuli have been suggested to mimic a distant predator.
source: which have been suggested to mimic a distant predator (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: Neurons in the pulvinar and parabigeminal nucleus respond well to quickly expanding dark stimuli, which are thought to mimic a quickly approaching threat.
source: In addition, neurons in the pulvinar and parabigeminal nucleus respond well to quickly expanding dark stimuli, which are thought to mimic a quickly approaching threat (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Dean et al., 1989; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and supported by citations to published literature (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Dean et al., 1989; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).

claim: Robust responses to approaching stimuli have been reported in both pulvinar-projecting and parabigeminal-projecting collicular neurons.
source: While robust responses to approaching stimuli have been reported in both pulvinar-projecting and parabigeminal-projecting collicular neurons
evidence: The claim is based on inference from published literature about collicular neuron responses.

claim: Only pulvinar-projecting collicular neurons have been reported to respond to small slowly moving stimuli.
source: only pulvinar-projecting collicular neurons have been reported to respond to small slowly moving stimuli (Beltramo and Scanziani, 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Gale and Murphy, 2016; Gale and Murphy, 2014; Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Maaten and Hinton, 2008; Inayat et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The putative ganglion cell types preferentially sampled by the colliculo-pulvinar circuit have smaller dendritic fields.
source: Consistent with these results, we found that the putative ganglion cell types preferentially sampled by the colliculo-pulvinar circuit have smaller dendritic fields
evidence: The claim is based on morphological measurements from the data.

claim: Fmini-OFF cells (cluster 2) respond to small, dark stimuli.
source: including the Fmini-OFF cells (cluster 2), which respond to small, dark stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on physiological recordings and known properties of this cell type.

claim: Cluster 10 could correspond to the local ON-cells (G17) based on small dendritic size and transient responses to a moving bar.
source: In addition, the pulvinar receives strong input from cluster 10, which based on the small dendritic size and transient responses to a moving bar (Bae et al., 2018) could correspond to the local ON-cells (G17) (Baden et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is based on morphological and physiological data and comparison with published cell types (Bae et al., 2018; Baden et al., 2016).

claim: Transient OFF-alpha cells (cluster 6) are known to preferentially respond to expanding stimuli.
source: Transient OFF-alpha cells (cluster 6) are known to preferentially respond to expanding stimuli and could mediate these responses in both circuits (Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015).

claim: Retinal ganglion cells with a bias for the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit have larger dendritic fields.
source: Retinal ganglion cells with a bias for the colliculo-parabigeminal circuit have larger dendritic fields
evidence: The claim is based on morphological measurements from the data.

claim: The putative function of parabigeminal-preferring ganglion cells is to respond to large moving objects and their motion direction (clusters 4, 7 and 13).
source: and their putative function is to respond to large moving objects and their motion direction (clusters 4, 7 and 13)
evidence: The claim is based on physiological recordings and inference about functional properties.

claim: Studies investigating the organization of retinal inputs to single cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus have suggested that there is a large degree of fuzziness/variability in the information each neuron receives from the retina.
source: Studies investigating the organization of retinal inputs to single cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus have suggested that there is a large degree of fuzziness/variability in the information each neuron receives from the retina (Hammer et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2018; Morgan et al., 2016; Rompani et al., 2017; Roson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the superior colliculus a high degree of regularity exists if one considers the projection targets.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in the superior colliculus a high degree of regularity exists if one considers the projection targets.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings from this study showing projection-specific sampling patterns.

claim: Each output pathway of the superior colliculus has access to a distinct, only partially overlapping, set of visual information encoded by the retina.
source: This data suggests there are strict limits on the degree of mixing of retinal ganglion cell inputs that occurs in the superior colliculus, where each output pathway has access to a distinct, only partially overlapping, set of visual information encoded by the retina.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings from this study showing projection-specific sampling patterns.

claim: Cruz-Martin et al. suggest that direction-selective neurons are preferentially sampled by layer one projecting neurons of the thalamus.
source: When considering the layer-specific targets of the lateral geniculate nucleus in the visual cortex, Cruz-Martin et al. suggest that direction-selective neurons are preferentially sampled by layer one projecting neurons of the thalamus (Cruz-Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cruz-Martín et al., 2014).
